title: Things to Do in Savannah: Three Squares for a Curious Afternoon
description: Explore Monterey, Madison and Ellis squares on a Savannah outing that leaves time for the public spaces between historic buildings.
body:
Looking for things to do in Savannah that leave room to enjoy the city’s pace? Choose a few squares instead of trying to visit them all. Monterey Square, Madison Square and Ellis Square offer three public settings for an outing through the historic district.

This selection stays with the squares and surrounding streets. River Street can be a separate addition if you have the time and energy; it is not a required final leg.

1. Begin at Monterey Square

Monterey Square sits at Bull and Taylor Streets. Visit Savannah includes it in its official walking guide through the historic district.

Start by enjoying the public paths and the relationship between the square and the buildings around it. There is no need to identify every house before the place becomes interesting. A smaller area can hold your attention when you are not immediately checking how far away the next attraction is.

Plan the stop: This is an outdoor public-space visit. Surrounding homes, gardens and interiors are not automatically open to visitors. Keep to public paths and use crossings around the square.

2. Give Madison Square its own pause

Continue along the Bull Street corridor to Madison Square at Harris Street. It is another stop in the official walking guide, but there is no requirement to follow the guide’s full route.

Enjoy this square as its own place rather than treating it as a repetition of the last one. The setting around a public space changes how it feels to spend time there. If you are visiting with someone else, allow enough time for both of you to settle into the outing instead of moving as soon as the first photo is taken.

Plan the stop: Look at monuments respectfully from the paths and read interpretation where available. A monument’s presence is not the whole history of a place. Do not climb on it or use it as a prop.

3. Finish around Ellis Square

Ellis Square, near Barnard and West Bryan Streets, moves the outing toward the City Market area. The surrounding activity gives it a different setting from the squares along Bull Street.

Use an open part of the square as a place to pause before deciding whether you want to browse or eat nearby. This is a useful stopping point because the next choice can remain open. You do not have to turn every public-space visit into a purchase.

Plan the stop: Follow current event arrangements and keep routes through the square clear. Nearby businesses have their own hours. Do not assume a particular water feature, seat or performance will be available.

Plan a comfortable walk through the historic district

Monterey and Madison sit along Bull Street; Ellis is farther north and west. Use a current map for the connection rather than assuming all three are on one uninterrupted straight path. Allow about two to three hours as a flexible planning budget, including pauses and street crossings.

The outdoor stops need no attraction ticket. Food, transport and interior attractions are separate. Pavement condition, heat, rain and your group’s pace can all affect the outing. Plan for drinking water and breaks, and leave room to stop early.

If you add the riverfront afterward, check the approach carefully: the changes in level and historic surfaces can affect access. It is perfectly reasonable to finish at Ellis Square and save the waterfront for another part of your visit.

Make a few squares part of your own story

SideQuest’s Savannah City Edition includes activities at these three places. It offers playful ways to engage with the surroundings, giving a familiar sightseeing walk a more personal direction. Download SideQuest and look for Savannah. The quest details can wait until you get there.
